The attic smelled of dust and forgotten summers. Lira knelt on the warped boards, flashlight beam cutting through motes that danced like slow insects. Her fingers found the loose plank by accident—she had been looking for her grandmother’s old sewing box—and when she pried it up the book waited underneath, wrapped in a scrap of oilcloth the color of dried blood. The cloth crackled when she unfolded it. The cover beneath was plain calfskin, no title, only a single dent where a thumb had rested for years.

She carried it downstairs because the attic felt suddenly crowded. At the kitchen table she lit the lamp her father had rewired last winter and opened the book to the first page. The paper was thick, almost cloth, and the ink had not faded. The first line read: You are already late. She laughed once, a small sound, and turned the page. Blank. Every page after that was blank except for faint horizontal rules, as if someone had prepared the book for a long confession and then lost the nerve.

Rain began against the windows. Lira set her elbow on the table and rested her chin in her hand. She had come home three weeks ago after the city job ended without ceremony. The garden needed weeding. The roof leaked in two places. Her mother wrote from the coast every Sunday and never asked when Lira would visit. The blank pages seemed, in that moment, like an accusation and an invitation at once.

She found a pencil in the drawer—soft lead, already sharpened by someone else—and wrote the second sentence without planning it: The train had left the station while I was still buying coffee. The words looked ordinary. She wrote another: I stood on the platform with the cup cooling in my hand and watched the lights shrink. A third: Somewhere in the second carriage a child was crying and no one answered.

The kitchen grew quieter. The rain softened to a mist that beaded on the glass. Lira kept writing because stopping felt harder than continuing. She described the coffee—too sweet, the lid not quite sealed—so a drop ran down her wrist and into the cuff of her coat. She described the timetable board flickering, a delay announced and then canceled. She gave the crying child a name she had never used before, Mara, and decided the mother had fallen asleep with her head against the window. None of this had happened to Lira. She had never missed a train for coffee. Yet the sentences arrived already warm, as if they had been waiting in the pencil.

Hours passed. The lamp buzzed. Her wrist ached. When she finally looked up the windows were black and the house had settled into its nighttime sounds: the refrigerator, a pipe ticking, the soft expansion of wood. Twenty-three pages were filled. She read the last paragraph aloud to hear how it landed. In it the woman on the platform—still unnamed—had begun to walk along the tracks because the next train was not scheduled until morning and she could not bear the waiting room’s fluorescent hum. Gravel shifted under her shoes. Far ahead a signal light changed from red to green for no train at all.

Lira set the pencil down. Her reflection in the dark window looked older than she felt, or perhaps simply more attentive. She turned back to the first page and saw that the original line, You are already late, had been absorbed into the new text; the letters were the same but now they belonged to the woman walking the tracks. The book had made room.

She made tea she did not drink. She walked through the house turning off lights she did not remember turning on. In her childhood bedroom the bed was still made with the quilt her grandmother had pieced from dresses no one wore anymore. Lira sat on the edge and opened the book again. The pencil felt lighter. She wrote until the woman reached a small station that was not on any map she knew, a platform lit by a single bulb, a bench occupied by an old man reading a newspaper whose date kept changing whenever he turned a page. The woman sat beside him. They did not speak. After a while the man folded the paper and offered her half a sandwich wrapped in waxed paper. She accepted. The bread was rye. The filling was something sharp and green she could not name.

Lira’s own stomach growled. She had forgotten dinner. Downstairs the kettle had gone cold. She carried the book with her and ate standing at the counter—bread, cheese, an apple—while the story continued in her head even though her hands were busy. When she returned to the pencil the woman and the old man were sharing the apple she had just eaten; the detail had crossed over without her noticing. She let it stand. Some thefts improve the original.

By two in the morning the woman had learned the old man’s name—Edwin—and the reason the station existed: it appeared only for people who had missed something important and were willing to walk toward the next uncertainty instead of back to the timetable. Edwin had been there for years, or for an afternoon; he was no longer sure. He tended a small stove in the stationmaster’s office and kept a ledger of arrivals that never listed departures. Lira wrote his handwriting as spidery and patient. She gave him a limp from an old fall and a habit of humming tunes whose words he had forgotten.

The rain stopped. A wind moved through the trees behind the house, and the sound entered the station as the clack of a distant signal arm. Lira felt the pull of sleep but also the sharper pull of the unfinished page. She wrote the woman asking Edwin whether anyone ever left. He considered the question for a long time, longer than the scene seemed able to hold, and finally said that leaving was easy if you remembered what you had been carrying when you arrived. Most people, he said, set their burdens down on the platform and then could not recall which coat was theirs.

Lira looked at her own hands. Graphite shadowed the side of her palm. She flexed her fingers and wrote one more sentence before she allowed herself to stop: She checked her pockets and found them empty except for the ticket stub she had never used. The period sat there, small and decisive. She closed the book. The cover was warm.

In bed she listened to the house. Somewhere a clock ticked, though she owned no clock that ticked. She thought of the garden that still needed weeding, of the two leaks in the roof, of her mother’s unasked question. None of those facts had entered the story, yet they felt lighter, as if the blank pages had taken some of their weight and transformed it into gravel under someone else’s shoes. She did not know whether she would finish the book or whether the book would finish itself while she slept. Both possibilities seemed tolerable.

Just before dawn she woke once, certain she had heard a train. The sound was already fading, a low metallic sigh moving away through the valley. She lay still and did not reach for the book on the nightstand. In the dark she could feel the shape of the next sentence waiting, patient as Edwin’s ledger, already half-formed, already hers and not hers. Outside, the first birds began, ordinary and exact. Lira closed her eyes and let the unfinished tracks continue without her for a little while longer, trusting they would still be there when the light arrived and her hands remembered the pencil.

message.reasoning:
The user said: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you."
The morning light filtered through the cracked window of my apartment, casting long shadows across the cluttered floor. I lay there, staring at the ceiling, feeling the familiar weight of another day pressing down on me. The alarm clock blinked 7:15, a harsh reminder that time doesn't pause for anyone, not even for those 1000 words. I sat up, rubbed my eyes, and let my mind wander. What comes to me now? The words on the page, the thoughts swirling in my head, they all blend together like ink in water.

I remembered the last time I tried to write something meaningful. It was a story about a 1000-word essay on the nature of time, but it turned into a rambling mess. Now, here I am, forced to produce exactly that length. The instruction sits there, "You have 1000 words," like a challenge or a trap. I need to fill it up without feeling rushed, without the pressure of counting every syllable.
